questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the level contour of the first tone in a one-syllable word
questions.stem: A teacher drills the four tones on a single syllable, writing it four times as ma1, ma2, ma3 and ma4. Which contour does the first of those four, used in the word for mother, actually have?

options.text: A level high pitch, held steady with no rise and no fall at all
A low start that climbs to a higher level and then stays there
options.misconception: confuses the level contour with the rising contour of tone two

options.text: A mid-high start that dips down low and then climbs again
options.misconception: confuses the level contour with the dipping contour of tone three

options.text: A high start that falls sharply through the middle down to a low level
options.misconception: confuses the level contour with the falling contour of tone four

questions.explanation: The word for mother is written with the first tone, and the first tone is level: the voice sits high on the syllable and neither rises nor falls, which is why it is charted as a straight line at about 55 on a five-degree scale. The three contours beside it are tones two, three and four in the same order a chart prints them, which is why a learner who has only met the four marks in a row tends to read a rise, a dip or a fall into the level mark. Nothing in the mark itself says level; the contour is a habit of the voice that has to be practised, and a first-tone syllable carried at a low or dipping pitch is heard as a different word.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to the pitch if the speaker held the syllable at the same height from start to finish.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the rising contour of the second tone in a one-syllable word
questions.stem: In the word for hemp, the syllable ma is written with a rising mark and the speaker's voice clearly climbs. What is the name of that tone and the shape of its pitch contour?

options.text: Tone two, which starts in the middle and rises to a high level
Tone one, which starts high and holds a level pitch for the whole syllable
options.misconception: reads a climbing voice as the level contour of tone one

options.text: Tone three, which starts low, dips and then climbs back to the middle
options.misconception: reads a simple climb as the dipping contour of tone three

options.text: Tone four, which starts high and falls all the way down to a low level
options.misconception: reads a rising voice as the falling contour of tone four

questions.explanation: The second tone is a rise: the voice begins around the middle of the speaker's range and climbs, so the word for hemp is heard as a clear upward glide. The mark above the vowel, a rising accent, names that shape, and the contour is charted as about 35 on a five-degree scale. A learner often swaps the second and the third tone, because both involve movement and both are described as having a bend in them, but the third tone goes down before it comes up while the second only ever goes up. Hearing the difference is easier than producing it, since the third tone is the one that asks the voice to start low and stay low for a moment.
questions.hint: Ask whether the voice ever moves downwards in the syllable you just heard.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: describe the dipping contour of the third tone and where the voice travels
questions.stem: A speaker says the word for horse, the syllable ma with a mark that falls and then rises, and the pitch clearly sinks below where it began. How is that contour properly described?

options.text: Tone three, a dipping shape that falls to a low point and rises again
Tone two, a smooth upward glide that starts low and ends at a high level
options.misconception: collapses the dip and the rise of tone three into a single climb

options.text: Tone one, a level hold on a high pitch with no movement inside the word
options.misconception: hears a level tone where the voice visibly drops and lifts again

options.text: Tone four, a clear fall from a high start straight down to a low ending
options.misconception: ignores the upward part of the third tone's contour

questions.explanation: The third tone is a dip: the voice starts around the middle, falls to the bottom of its range, and comes back up, which is why the mark is drawn as a check that falls and rises. The word for horse is the standard example, and its contour is charted as about 214, the extra digit recording how far the voice sank. The temptation is to treat every moving tone as a simple two-part shape, which collapses the third into the second or the fourth, and the cost of that collapse is immediate: the same syllable with a different tone is a different word, so a speaker who says the word for horse with a rising voice has said the word for hemp.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate movements the voice makes inside that one syllable.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the falling contour of the fourth tone in a one-syllable word
questions.stem: The word for scold is written with a falling mark, and the pitch of the voice begins near the top of the range and drops decisively. Which tone does that combination represent in Mandarin?

options.text: Tone four, a falling contour that begins high and finishes at a low level
Tone three, a dipping contour that ends as high as the syllable began
options.misconception: hears the fourth tone as a dip that returns upward

options.text: Tone one, a level contour held at a high pitch with no movement at all
options.misconception: hears a falling voice as a syllable held flat and high

options.text: Tone two, a rising contour that begins low and finishes at a high level
options.misconception: reads the direction of the fall as though it were a rise

questions.explanation: The fourth tone is a fall, and the mark above the vowel is drawn as a stroke that descends from left to right, matching what the voice does. It is charted as about 51, where the first digit is the high start and the second is the low end, so the pair of numbers tells a speaker both how high to begin and how low to finish. The trap here is a learner who hears only that the syllable is not flat and reaches for the dipping third tone, but the third tone returns upward at the end while the fourth tone simply stops, and the second tone only ever climbs.
questions.hint: Ask what the last thing the voice does inside the syllable is.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: recognise the neutral tone on the suffix of a noun such as the word for table
questions.stem: A learner meets the word for table, written zhuozi, and hears the second syllable fall in pitch and carry no tone mark at all. What is happening in that second syllable?

options.text: It takes the neutral tone, a short syllable read flat and unstressed
It takes the second tone, because some printing fonts draw it without a mark
options.misconception: believes an unmarked syllable must be hiding a rising tone

options.text: It takes the fourth tone, because a falling mark is dropped before a noun
options.misconception: treats the missing mark as an abbreviated fourth tone

options.text: It takes the first tone, because a level pitch is easier for a beginner to hear
options.misconception: chooses a numbered tone on the grounds that it is easier to produce

questions.explanation: The word for table is built on a suffix that behaves like a grammatical particle rather than a full syllable of its own, so it is read with the neutral tone: short, light, and without a tone mark, which is how a writer shows there is no numbered tone there. The same suffix appears in the words for chair, plate and bottle, and the same light reading appears in words such as friend, where the second syllable also loses its own contour. A learner who supplies a numbered tone is not mispronouncing by accident, they are treating a suffix as if it carried the same weight as the noun in front of it, and that is why the resulting syllable sounds heavy where a speaker's would sound light.
questions.hint: Ask whether that second syllable could be stressed if the speaker chose to stress it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: conclude that tone alone can separate several unrelated words
questions.stem: A beginner's flashcard shows four items whose pinyin is identical apart from the tone: the first means mother, the second hemp, the third horse and the fourth to scold. What does that card demonstrate?

options.text: Tone alone separates four unrelated words that share one syllable
Each character must carry a different initial before the tone can matter
options.misconception: believes tone only counts once the initial consonant has changed

options.text: Characters are written in pinyin first and only receive tones afterwards
options.misconception: thinks tone is a later addition to a finished syllable

options.text: The same written syllable can never stand for more than one word
options.misconception: assumes one syllable can hold only one meaning in the language

questions.explanation: These four words share one syllable, one initial and one final, and nothing distinguishes them but the contour, which is why a learner who hears the syllable without the tone cannot know which word has been said. Each of the four is written with a different character, so the characters are also different, but the characters are learned together with the reading, and the reading is what carries the contrast in speech. The tempting belief is that a syllable is a fixed label for one meaning, and it produces a learner who pronounces all four words alike, which a speaker hears as a running commentary of unrelated meanings in one breath.
questions.hint: Ask what information is left over once you have removed the tone from those four entries.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: apply the tone change between two dipping tones in one word
questions.stem: A speaker says the two syllables of the greeting for hello, both of them dipping, and the first syllable comes out rising instead. What rule turns that written dipping tone into a rising one?

options.text: Two dipping tones in a row, with the first one sounded as a rising tone
Two rising tones in a row, with the second one sounded as a level tone
options.misconception: invents a rule for two rising tones that the language does not have

options.text: A neutral tone after a falling tone, with the first one left unstressed
options.misconception: explains a rising first syllable by a neutral-tone rule instead

options.text: A change that applies only after the particle at the end of a clause
options.misconception: believes the shift waits until a final particle is reached

questions.explanation: When two dipping tones fall next to each other, the first one is sounded as a rising tone, so the greeting written with two dipping marks is heard with a rise on the first syllable. The reason is mechanical rather than decorative: two syllables that both sink leave the ear with a falling contour to climb back out of, and speaking the first one as a rise gives the pair a workable shape. The written marks do not change, only the sound does, and that is the detail a learner misses. A speaker who keeps both dipping marks exactly as written produces a greeting that is heard but not recognised.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when two syllables both want to sink in a row.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: apply the rule that decides which vowel in a syllable carries the tone mark
questions.stem: A typing rule has to decide which vowel carries the mark in a syllable written with iu or with ui at the end. Which statement describes the convention actually used?

options.text: Mark a before o before e, and otherwise mark the later of i and u
Always mark the first vowel of the syllable, whatever the order is
options.misconception: marks the first vowel and misplaces the mark on every iu and ui

options.text: Mark the vowel that is pronounced for the longest time in the syllable
options.misconception: thinks tone placement depends on how long a vowel is held

options.text: Leave the mark off i and u and write the tone as a separate digit
options.misconception: believes the tones are written as numerals instead of marks

questions.explanation: A tone mark goes over a when a syllable has one, otherwise over o, otherwise over e, and only when the syllable offers just i and u does the rule pick the second of the two. That last case is why six is written with the mark over the u and four is written with the mark over the i. The rule exists because a single mark cannot sit over two vowels, and the language resolved the collision by naming one of them. A learner who marks the first vowel produces a written form that a reader will read as a different syllable, so the mistake does not stay a spelling slip: it points at another word.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two vowels in a closing iu or ui is the one that sounds.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what the unmarked fifth slot on a tone chart stands for
questions.stem: A grammar chart draws a fifth slot underneath the four numbered tones and leaves it without any mark. Which real use of that slot does the chart describe?

options.text: A short unstressed syllable read flat and briefly, with no tone mark
A long stressed syllable read at a middle level with no mark at all
options.misconception: thinks an unmarked slot still means a long and prominent syllable

options.text: A syllable whose pitch is left entirely to the hearer's own choice
options.misconception: believes the fifth slot means the pitch is not fixed at all

options.text: A clause-final syllable that always rises to ask the listener a question
options.misconception: confuses the neutral tone with the rise of a spoken question

questions.explanation: The fifth slot on a Mandarin chart is the neutral tone, and it is not a fifth contour but the absence of a contour: the syllable is short, light, and carried at a middling pitch without any of the four shapes. It is written with no mark at all, and a speaker supplies whatever small pitch the surrounding syllables leave room for. The slot is used in two kinds of place, inside compounds whose second syllable is a suffix, and on grammatical words such as the question particle and the sentence-final particle when they are not stressed. A learner who treats the slot as a licence to choose any pitch produces something that sounds like an extra syllable rather than a light one.
questions.hint: Ask how long the syllable is and how much stress it is given.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: conclude that tone is part of the syllable's pronunciation and not a decoration on it
questions.stem: A dictionary lists one character with two readings, one glossed as long and the other as to grow. What does that single character show about how meaning is encoded?

options.text: Tone belongs to the pronunciation of the syllable, not to the character alone
A character keeps exactly one reading, so the second entry is a mistake
options.misconception: believes a written character can only ever be read one way

options.text: Meaning is carried by the tone mark alone, and never by the rest of the syllable
options.misconception: thinks tone is the whole of the pronunciation rather than part of it

options.text: Different readings always require different characters inside the same word
options.misconception: expects the writing to change whenever the reading changes

questions.explanation: One written character is read here as a long thing and there as the act of growing, and the two readings are told apart by the pitch contour rather than by any change of initial or final. Tone is therefore part of what a syllable is, not a mark added to it afterwards, and this is why a learner who reads a character with one fixed pitch will meet words whose meaning has nothing to do with the one they know. The character's own history explains the second reading: a word for an elder who is respected in a family began as a word for the one who is grown up, and the grown-up sense is the one that survives.
questions.hint: Ask what is the same in both entries and what is the only thing that differs.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: split a written syllable into its initial and its final
questions.stem: A learner is told to split a Mandarin syllable into an initial sound and a final. For the syllable written with z, h and an ong ending, what is the initial?

options.text: The two letters zh, a sound made with the tongue tip curled back
The single letter z, a sound made with the tongue tip flat against the teeth
options.misconception: drops the h and hears an ordinary affricate instead of the curled one

options.text: The whole ending ong, which is a final and not a consonant at all
options.misconception: takes a final for an initial because it is the longest part

options.text: Nothing at all, since the syllable happens to begin with a vowel sound
options.misconception: misreads a written consonant as though no consonant were present

questions.explanation: The syllable in question is written with two letters for its initial, and those two letters stand for one consonant sound, produced with the tip of the tongue curled back against the roof of the mouth. The rest of the syllable, ending in an open nasal sound, is the final. Mandarin initials are a closed list, and three of them are written with two letters because each is a single sound that an alphabet with one letter per sound cannot spell. A learner who writes only the first letter has not simplified the spelling, they have changed the sound, and the result is a different syllable with a different word attached to it.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate consonant sounds the two letters stand for.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why a syllable can be written with no letter at all before its vowel
questions.stem: The syllable for love is written as a vowel with a falling mark and no letter standing before it. How does the writing system account for that shape?

options.text: The initial is empty, and the final carries the whole sound of the syllable
A letter was left out because the tone mark took the space it needed
options.misconception: believes the writing lost a letter to make room for the tone

options.text: A glottal stop was intended and the writer simply did not type it
options.misconception: reads the unmarked slot as an untyped consonant letter

options.text: The shape appears only when the syllable also carries a tone mark
options.misconception: ties the absence of a letter to the presence of a tone

questions.explanation: Many Mandarin syllables have no consonant at the start, and pinyin writes that by beginning the syllable straight away with the vowel, so the analysis of the syllable is an empty initial followed by a final. The word for love is one of them, and so is the syllable for one. Phonetically a speaker does close the throat very slightly at the start of such a syllable, and descriptions differ about whether to call that a full consonant or an onset, but the writing system makes no letter for it, which is the point: a chart of initials has a slot for nothing and the syllables that use it are ordinary, not exceptional.
questions.hint: Ask how a chart would have to label a syllable whose first sound is not a consonant.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a back vowel in a final from a front vowel in the same slot
questions.stem: A learner mixes up the word for long and the word for orchid because the two finals look similar on paper. How does the language keep the vowel quality apart?

options.text: The back vowel in the first final has a different mouth shape from the front one
The two finals are actually identical, and only the tone marks tell them apart
options.misconception: reduces a vowel difference to a difference of contour

options.text: The difference is carried by the length of the final rather than by its vowel
options.misconception: hears a vowel-quality contrast as a length contrast

options.text: The difference exists in speech alone, and the pinyin spelling ignores it
options.misconception: believes the written finals fail to record a real sound difference

questions.explanation: The vowel written in the first of those finals is a back vowel: the tongue sits further back in the mouth, and the vowel of the second final is a front vowel, produced with the tongue further forward. The two are neighbours on the vowel chart and are easy to confuse for a speaker of a language with no such pairs, but the difference is exactly what separates a large family of syllables, including the words for long and for orchid. The reason the spelling looks similar is that the letters are doing the same job in both, marking the vowel and a following nasal; what differs is the position the tongue takes, and pinyin does record it even where the letters look alike.
questions.hint: Ask where the tip of the tongue sits in each of the two syllables.

questions.learningObjective: identify the one candidate syllable the phonotactic constraints rule out
questions.stem: A generator offers four candidate syllables for a practice exercise, and one of them can be pronounced by no standard speaker. Which one is that?

options.text: A syllable beginning with a ch sound and ending in the eng final

options.misconception: believes no syllable may end in a nasal vowel at all

options.text: A syllable beginning with an sh sound and ending in the uo final
options.misconception: thinks the curled consonant cannot be followed by a plain vowel

options.text: A syllable beginning with a c sound and ending in the ong final
options.misconception: assumes a forbidden combination exists for every consonant class

A learner who assumes the pattern is regular will try to pronounce it, and a listener will hear an attempt rather than a word.
questions.hint: Ask which nasal ending the three retracted initials refuse, and which one they accept.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: supply the two dots that a nasal-initial-free vowel requires in writing
questions.stem: A learner's dictionary prints the character used in the word for roughly as a final with a plain u and a falling tone. What does the spelling rule actually require there?

options.text: The u carries two dots, because nothing else in the syllable hides the vowel
The u is written plain, because the two dots are only used after a j
options.misconception: moves the rule about plain u to the wrong set of initials

options.text: The u is written with no tone mark, because a front vowel takes no tone
options.misconception: believes the two dots replace the tone mark in this final

options.text: The u is doubled to two letters, because one letter cannot hold that vowel
options.misconception: thinks a single vowel needs a doubled letter to be written

questions.explanation: The vowel in that final is a front rounded vowel, and pinyin writes it as a u with two dots above it. The dots can be left off in exactly one situation, which is after the three initials written with a flat tongue against the palate, where the writing already has a letter that would be read ambiguously without them, so the pair keeps the plain u instead. Everywhere else the dots must be written, which is why the character used in the word for roughly carries them and the word for decide does not. A learner who drops the dots in the first case has written a different syllable, and a learner who keeps them in the second has written one no speaker would produce.
questions.hint: Ask which initials earn the right to write a plain u, and what the rest of the syllables must do.

questions.learningObjective: let context choose between two readings of an ambiguous character

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why a plain u is written after one set of initials and a dotted u elsewhere
questions.stem: A learner writes the word for decide with a plain u, which is correct there, but writes the same plain u in a word beginning with an l, which is not. What is the spelling convention doing?

options.text: After three initials the plain u stands for the same vowel the dots mark elsewhere
After three initials the u stands for a different vowel that needs no dots at all
options.misconception: believes the plain u after those initials is a different sound

options.text: The u is doubled after every consonant, so the two letters stand for one sound
options.misconception: treats a doubled vowel letter as the way to write the sound

options.text: The two dots are written on the initial instead, marking the same front vowel
options.misconception: moves the dots onto the consonant rather than onto the vowel

Where a syllable begins with one of the three initials written with a flat tongue against the palate, the u is already unambiguous, because those initials never take a back vowel, so the writer drops the dots and the sound stays the same one. Everywhere else the two dots are needed, because a plain u would otherwise be read as the back vowel it usually carries. The result is one vowel with two spellings, and a learner who learns the sound once and the spelling as a rule will not have to memorise two separate things.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate the claim that a glide in the written spelling counts as an initial
questions.stem: A pinyin chart lists the letter y among the initials, yet a linguist objects that it is not one. What is the objection based on?

The letter is a tone mark that has been misread as a consonant
options.misconception: confuses an initial letter with the tone mark above a vowel

options.text: The letter is a final that has been written at the front of the word
options.misconception: reverses the two halves of a syllable and treats the front as the end

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the classifier that stands between a number and a noun
questions.stem: A learner wants to say three books and writes the number, then the noun, with nothing in between. What does the language put in the gap, and what is that word called?

options.text: A classifier, so a number, then a classifier, then the noun, in that order
Nothing at all, because Mandarin numbers stand directly in front of nouns
options.misconception: believes a bare number before a noun is complete and natural

options.text: A possessive particle, which turns the number into an owner of the noun
options.misconception: reads the middle slot as a possessive rather than a classifier

options.text: A preposition, which is required before the noun in every counted phrase
options.misconception: expects a locative preposition between a number and a noun

questions.explanation: Counted nouns take three parts in a fixed order: the number, then a classifier that tells you what shape of thing is being counted, then the noun. The classifier for book-shaped things is the one used in three books, and a different noun takes a different classifier, so the middle slot cannot simply be left empty. One general classifier does exist and is used constantly, especially for things with no obvious shape class of their own, but a learner who reaches for it every time sounds vague rather than wrong, and native speakers notice the vagueness. The order itself is the part that is fixed and the part that a learner most often gets wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the language would like to know about the noun besides how many there are.

questions.learningObjective: choose a classifier by the class of the noun being counted
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say one cat and one sheet of paper. Which pair of classifiers does the language expect for those two nouns?

options.text: The same general classifier for both, since that is the only one a learner needs
options.misconception: believes one general classifier covers every kind of counted noun

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach what the pitch contour of a syllable contributes to the writing system
questions.stem: A learner asks why the pitch of a syllable matters as much as its consonants and its finals, and what would be lost if every syllable were read at one flat level. Explain what the contour does, and why one syllable can carry several unrelated meanings.

answer.exemplar: The contour is part of what a syllable is, not a decoration added to it. Mandarin has four numbered tones, each with its own shape: one level and high, two rising from the middle, three dipping down before it comes back up, and four falling from high to low, plus a neutral reading used for short unstressed syllables such as the suffix in the word for table. The reason this matters is that the inventory of syllables is small compared with the number of words, so the same syllable is reused many times over and the tone is often the only thing telling two of them apart: the syllable written with a level tone is mother, with a rising tone is hemp, with a dipping tone is horse, and with a falling tone is to scold, four unrelated words sharing one sound. Read everything at a flat level and the language loses the ability to distinguish those words, and a listener hears a run of syllables with no way of knowing where one word ended. Two further points are worth making. First, the written mark does not always show what is heard, because two dipping tones in a row are spoken with a rise on the first one, so the greeting for hello is written with two dipping marks and said with a rise and a dip. Second, the neutral reading is not a fifth contour but the absence of one: it is short and light, which is why a suffix such as the one in the word for chair is written with no mark at all.

questions.explanation: This item asks a learner to teach the whole tone system rather than one tone, which is where the real difficulty sits: the contours are easy to recognise one at a time and hard to hold in the head as a single set that a speaker switches between without thinking. The teaching move that works is to start from the reuse of syllables, because once a learner has heard that one syllable carries four unrelated words, the contours stop being an arbitrary list and become the thing that keeps those words apart. The neutral reading and the change between two dipping tones both need naming explicitly, since a learner who leaves them out will produce speech that is heard but not recognised.
questions.hint: Ask what would be left to distinguish words if the pitch never moved at all.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach how three alike-sounding particles are told apart by position
questions.stem: A learner is told that three different particles are written with different characters but sound alike in careful speech, and has to choose between them by position alone. Explain what each one does, and how anyone can tell which to write.

answer.exemplar: The rule is positional, and the three jobs are told apart by what stands on each side of the particle. Before a noun and after a modifier, the particle links the two, as in a red thing where the red comes first, and it is the same one that closes a relative clause: the person who buys books is written with the noun first, then the verb, then this particle, then the head noun. In front of a verb and after an adjective, a differently written particle makes an adverbial phrase, so a slow walk becomes the adverbial phrase placed before the verb that means to walk. After a verb or an adjective, the third particle is a complement that says how far something went, as in run fast or speak well, and it needs something on its left that can be measured, which is why it cannot follow a noun. The practical consequence for a speaker is that the decision is made by looking at the structure, not by listening, because in connected speech the three are frequently not pronounced apart at all. A useful check for a learner is to ask two questions: is the thing on my left a noun, or is it a verb or an adjective, and is the thing on my right another noun, or a verb. A noun on the left plus a noun on the right gives the linking particle; an adjective on the left plus a verb on the right gives the adverbial one; and a verb or an adjective on the left with nothing measurable after it yet gives the complement.

questions.explanation: The reason this trio defeats learners is that the distinction is invisible in speech, so the usual method of learning by ear cannot work and the position has to become the deciding clue. A teaching explanation should therefore be built around the two questions about the neighbours of the particle, because that is a procedure a learner can apply to a sentence they have never seen. It is also worth saying plainly that the three are often not pronounced separately even when they are written apart, which stops a learner from hunting for a difference in the sound that is not there to be found.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of word stands on each side of the particle in the sentence in front of you.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach what the two markers contribute and why they reorder the clause
questions.stem: A learner asks why this language needs two separate markers when one sentence of English can simply say who did what to whom. Explain what each marker contributes, and why the word order changes when they appear.

answer.exemplar: Both markers point at the same thing, the object of the verb, and both put it in front, but they disagree about who the sentence is about. The disposal marker leaves the doer as the subject and moves the object forward, so the order is subject, marker, object, verb: I put the book on the desk. Because the marker announces a known object, the object has to be something both speakers can already identify, which is why it works so well with verbs of eating, buying and finishing, and why putting a brand new object straight into that frame sounds odd. The passive marker does the opposite with the object: it takes over the subject position itself, so the sentence begins with the thing that was acted on and the doer, if it is named at all, comes after the marker: the door was broken by him, or simply the door was broken, with nobody named. That is why the two markers cannot be interchanged freely: one keeps the doer in charge of the sentence and the other removes them from the front, and the reason a translation so often feels clumsy is that a single English sentence has to choose one point of view while the two Chinese forms offer it a choice.

questions.explanation: The value of teaching the pair together is that the two are not opposites but two answers to the same question, and a learner who sees them side by side stops treating the passive as the odd one out. The object-before-verb order is the mechanical part and has to be stated plainly, because it is what a learner gets wrong when the meaning is understood. The definiteness condition on the disposal marker is the part that is usually skipped and the part that explains why the construction feels constrained once the learner starts writing longer sentences.

questions.learningObjective: teach what a classifier contributes and how one is chosen
questions.stem: A learner asks why a number cannot sit in front of a noun on its own, and why one general classifier is not a complete answer to the question. Explain what a classifier contributes, how one is chosen, and where the general one still fits.

answer.exemplar: A counted noun takes three parts in a fixed order: the number, then a classifier, then the noun, as in three books, one cat and one sheet of paper. The classifier is not filler, because it tells the listener what kind or shape of thing is being counted, and that is information the bare number does not carry: the same number is used before a cat, before a book and before a car, and only the middle word distinguishes them. Most classifiers are chosen by shape or kind, so animals take one, flat sheet-like things such as paper and tickets take another, long thin things such as fish and towels take a third, books take a fourth, vehicles take a fifth, and tools with handles take a sixth. There is also a general classifier which means a single one or a general unit, and it is genuinely useful: it is the right word for things that have no obvious shape class, for abstract nouns when they are counted at all, and for a speaker who simply has not learned the specific word yet. The problem with leaning on it all the time is that it flattens the picture. A learner who says the general classifier for everything produces sentences that are not wrong but are vaguer than they need to be, and choosing the specific classifier is one of the clearest signs that a noun vocabulary is becoming usable speech.

questions.explanation: The misconception to head off here is that a classifier is a grammatical ornament inserted between a number and a noun, and once a learner sees it as carrying the shape information the whole system stops feeling arbitrary. The general classifier needs an honest defence rather than a warning, because it is genuinely the right word in a number of places and a learner told only that it is lazy will overcorrect. The teaching order that works is shape first and general second, which is the order a learner meets them in real sentences.

questions.learningObjective: teach why subjects are dropped and why phrases are fronted
questions.stem: A learner asks why this language leaves out subjects in some sentences and puts phrases at the front that an English sentence would place at the end. Explain subjectless sentences and topic-comment structure, and say what each construction depends on.

answer.exemplar: Both patterns come from the same habit: the sentence is built around what the listener already has rather than around what the grammar would nominally require. A subject can be left out when the referent is obvious, and the most common cases are sentences about the weather, where there is nobody to name, sentences about a state of affairs, and sentences about an action whose doer is whoever is speaking, such as a report that the food is ready or that someone has arrived. The omission is licensed rather than random, and the test is whether the referent is known: when a new referent is being introduced for the first time, the subject has to be said. Topic-comment structure works the same way in a different slot. A known subject is placed in front as the topic, telling the listener what the sentence is about, and the new information comes behind it as the comment, often with a comma in writing and a small break in speech. The pattern is extremely common, and it is why a translator who expects a subject before the verb sometimes finds none. Its practical value is that it lets a speaker hold an idea in view across a long sentence, repeating the topic later if it needs to, and that repetition is one of the main reasons the language tolerates a missing subject in the first place.

questions.explanation: These two patterns look unrelated to a learner and are in fact the same principle applied to two different slots, so an explanation that puts them side by side does more work than two separate descriptions. The point to insist on is that both are conditioned: the subject is dropped only when the referent is known, and the topic is fronted only when the listener can be assumed to follow it. A learner who thinks the subject can be dropped whenever it likes will produce sentences whose referent has to be guessed, which is the real cost of not learning the condition.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach how time and change are reported without verb inflection
questions.stem: A learner asks how this language reports time and change when the verb never changes its form. Explain the two jobs of the particle le, and show how the position of a time word changes what a clause reports.

answer.exemplar: Chinese verbs do not inflect for tense, so time and change are carried by other means, and the particle le is the biggest of them. Attached to a verb, it says the action is finished and can be treated as a whole, which is why it appears with a time expression giving how long the activity lasted: he was away for three days, with the same particle at the end of the verb saying the stay is over. Placed at the end of the clause instead, it reports a change of situation, a new state that the listener did not have before: it is raining now, the sky has gone light, I am about to leave. The two can appear in one sentence, once after the verb and once at the end, and that is the clearest evidence that they are two faces of one particle. A time word does a second kind of work. Placed in front of the whole clause it frames the sentence, telling the listener to hold that stretch of time in mind while the rest is read, so yesterday I went to the museum reports that the going happened inside that frame. Placed between the subject and the verb it becomes one piece of information among others about the activity. A learner who puts a time word at the end, after the object, has not made a stylistic choice: that position is not available, and the clause has to be rescued with a pause or rewritten.

Showing that the same particle can occupy both positions in a single sentence is worth the extra effort, because it makes the two functions feel like one thing with two shapes rather than two separate rules to memorise. The framing job of a fronted time word is the part that most often disappears in translation, and a learner who notices it will translate more accurately even without being able to explain it.

questions.learningObjective: diagnose the two uses of a particle and then move a sentence from one to the other
questions.stem: Stage one: a speaker says wo chi le after the word for food, and then says yao zou le at the end of the clause. Say which of the two uses of the particle each is. Stage two: rewrite the second sentence so the particle reports a finished stay instead of a new departure.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the first is the use attached to a verb, and it says the eating is finished and can be treated as a whole, so the sentence reports a completed meal. The second sits at the end of the clause with nothing after it, and it reports a change of situation, so the listener understands that a departure is now under way rather than merely possible. The two are the same particle and they can even both appear in one sentence, once after the verb and once at the end, which is the clearest sign they are two faces of one word. Stage two: to report a finished stay, the particle has to move to the verb and the clause needs a time phrase saying how long the stay lasted, as in he was away for three days, where the same particle now marks the end of a stretch of time instead of a change of state. Removing the clause-final particle is not enough on its own, because then the sentence simply reports a departure with no newness in it, and the time phrase is what gives the particle something to be bounded by.

questions.explanation: The second stage is harder than the first for the same reason every recasting task is: it asks the learner to give up a function the particle does well and find the other one, and the natural instinct is to delete the particle rather than to relocate it. Naming that instinct in the explanation saves a learner from the most common wrong answer. The useful observation for the learner is that the two uses are not two different words, which is why the same character can appear twice in a single sentence with two different jobs.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two sentences could take a time phrase saying how long, and what the other one is doing instead.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a construction and then recast the sentence with the other marker
questions.stem: Stage one: a speaker says xiao wang ba men xiu hao le and a colleague says men bei xiao wang xiu hao le about the same repair. Say which construction each sentence uses and what that does to the word order. Stage two: rewrite the first sentence as a passive, keeping the doer in the sentence.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the first is the disposal construction, in which the doer stays the subject and the known object is moved in front of the verb, so the order is subject, marker, object, verb. The second is the passive, in which the object takes over the front position and the doer is moved to the back behind the marker, so the order is object, marker, doer, verb. The same four participants are in both sentences, and the only change is whose point of view the sentence is told from: the first is about what the repairer achieved, the second about how the door ended up. Stage two: the passive version is the door was repaired by him, with the object first, then the marker, then the doer, then the verb and the completion particle. A learner who tries to keep the doer in the front position cannot, because the whole point of the passive is that the object takes that place, and a learner who simply deletes the marker has produced a third sentence that reports the door with no doer and no marker at all, which is grammatical and means something different.

questions.explanation: The diagnostic half of this task is the one that reveals whether a learner has learned the two markers as two shapes or as two arguments about the sentence, and the recasting half is where that shows. The trap worth naming is the deletion instinct: when a learner cannot get the passive to work with the doer in it, the easy move is to remove the marker, and the resulting sentence is acceptable but is no longer the construction that was asked for. Explaining that difference between an acceptable sentence and the right sentence is the part of the feedback that carries over to longer writing.
questions.hint: Ask which noun is standing in the front position, and whether that noun did the action.
